conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you. I understand you’re here with epigastric abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started again about four days ago. It feels like the ulcer pain I had last time—burning right in the middle. I’ve been nauseated and threw up dark yellow stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever or chills? Any blood in vomit, black stools, or new diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No blood. No black stools. I’m passing gas and had a bowel movement today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are you taking your ulcer medications—acid suppression and sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve been taking pantoprazole and sucralfate like I’m supposed to. They switched me to liquid omeprazole because they thought I wasn’t absorbing the pantoprazole. I started that yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your bypass and absorption issues. We’ll treat this like a flare of the marginal ulcer, but we also want to make sure there’s no perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think it could be a hole again? I’m scared of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now your vitals are stable and your labs don’t show a high white blood cell count, which is reassuring. We’re getting X-rays to look for free air, which would suggest a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also noticed more drainage around my G-tube this morning. It’s not red, but it’s wet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’ll examine the site and keep an eye on it. If there’s no redness, increasing pain, or fever, it’s often irritation or leakage, but we’ll make sure it looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I staying NPO again? I can’t really eat anyway because of the low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—nothing by mouth for now. We’ll continue your continuous tube feeds once we’ve ruled out anything dangerous on imaging. We’ll also give IV fluids and IV acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is pretty bad. What can I get for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give IV pain medication and anti-nausea medication now, and start IV pantoprazole to calm the ulcer irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back—no free air under the diaphragm and no acute lung issues. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This makes a perforation much less likely. We’re also doing abdominal X-rays to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is a little better after the meds, but I still feel that burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common early on. The IV pantoprazole can take some time to fully help. We’ll keep you comfortable and reassess frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I checked your labs: white blood cell count is normal, kidney function looks good, electrolytes are okay, and your lactate is normal. Those are all reassuring signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean it’s definitely the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It points toward an ulcer flare being the most likely cause, especially with your history and similar symptoms. Imaging helps us rule out emergencies like perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep my tube feeds running? I’m worried about my blood sugar dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the abdominal X-ray confirms no free air, we’ll resume your continuous tube feeds. We’ll also monitor your blood sugars while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back—no obstruction and no free air. It does show a mild to moderate stool burden, but nothing surgical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can restart the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart your continuous tube feeds and keep you NPO by mouth. We’ll continue IV pantoprazole and your sucralfate through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the drainage around the tube—could it be infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now the skin doesn’t look red or swollen, and you don’t have fever. We’ll keep it clean and dry and watch for changes. If it becomes painful, red, or foul-smelling, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or dry heaving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. I still feel queasy sometimes, but it’s better. The pain is less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your tube feeds are running okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m tolerating them. No cramping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole today and continue pain control as needed. We’ll also keep checking your blood sugars—so far they’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why do I keep getting these ulcers? I’m doing what I’m told.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Marginal ulcers can recur after Roux-en-Y because the connection between the stomach pouch and small intestine is sensitive to acid and irritation. Even with good medication use, some people are prone to them, and absorption can be tricky after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the liquid medicine is better for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often, yes—liquid or dissolvable forms can be absorbed more reliably in some patients after bypass. We’ll make sure your discharge plan uses a form you can take consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about taking too much pain medicine. I don’t want to be constipated or out of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good concern. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and pair it with a bowel regimen like docusate and senna if needed. We’ll also avoid anything that could worsen the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This evening, since you’re stable and not vomiting, we’ll start planning to transition you off IV medications when appropriate. For now, we’ll keep the IV pantoprazole going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I might go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your pain stays controlled, you tolerate tube feeds, and there’s no vomiting, discharge in the next day or two is possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your abdominal pain today compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. It’s still there, but not constant. I haven’t thrown up since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s what we hoped to see with IV acid suppression. We’ll keep you on continuous tube feeds and NPO by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least sip water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to stick with nothing by mouth because that’s been safest for your hypoglycemia management and to avoid irritating the ulcer. You’ll continue water flushes through the tube every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site is still leaking a little. Is that going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small amount of drainage can happen. As long as the skin stays healthy—no spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, or fever—we manage it with local care. If it worsens at home, you should call the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’ve been stable—no low blood sugars, tube feeds tolerated, and pain improved. Today we’ll focus on getting you ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will I be taking at home for the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue sucralfate four times a day through the tube, and we’ll send you home on an acid-suppressing medicine that’s easier to absorb—lansoprazole in an orally disintegrating form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not the pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we used IV pantoprazole because it works well and bypasses absorption issues. For home, we’re choosing a formulation that should work better for you without needing an IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scope like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not during this admission. Since you improved with medication and there were no signs of bleeding or perforation, we’re treating it medically and having you follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also sending a bowel regimen home—docusate, and senna or bisacodyl as needed—because pain medication can cause constipation and your X-ray showed some stool burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What pain medicine am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe hydromorphone to use only as needed for pain, with instructions not to drive or drink alcohol while taking it. The goal is to taper off as your ulcer pain settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any nausea or vomiting since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I feel a lot better. I’m just nervous it’ll come right back when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The key is staying consistent with the acid suppression and sucralfate, keeping tube feeds continuous as prescribed, and staying NPO by mouth as you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for severe or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, fever, or if the tube site becomes very red, painful, or starts draining pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you today. You’re stable, walking independently, tolerating continuous tube feeds, and your symptoms improved with IV antacid therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the plan one more time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sure: continue continuous tube feeds and remain nothing by mouth; take lansoprazole daily and sucralfate four times daily; use hydromorphone only as needed for pain; use docusate and senna/bisacodyl as needed for constipation; and follow up with your surgeons in clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you. I’ll keep an eye on the tube site and stick to the meds.
